title: Satyavati

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Bhishma's vow: a father's boon, death only with his son's leave. Who did you thank for something they gave up for you? Day seven hundred sixteen.
screen: `THE LONG LIFE IN HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell. He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river. This is where Satyavati's story begins.
screen: `A HAWK OVER THE YAMUNA.` → `A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.` → `IT FALLS INTO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls. Some time later, fishermen catch her, and when they cut her open, they find two human children inside, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends; she rises from the fish's body and goes back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king. And the king makes a choice. He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be a king named Matsya. The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen. Let her be your daughter, he says. She grows up beautiful, and she carries the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati. Now go back to the riverbank, a few days ago in our reading, when Shantanu asked who she was. I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she told him. Every word of that is true. The man who raised her is her father. But she's also a king's daughter, born from an apsara's body, handed away as a baby while her brother stayed in the palace. The poem gave us that half long ago, in its account of the ancestors, before she ever set foot in a boat. The fisherman who bargained so hard for her son's crown was bargaining for the child a king gave away. A king's daughter, a fisherman's child, rowing travelers across a river. She'll be a queen of the Kurus. But that's not where she started. Tomorrow we stay with her a little longer, before the palace, out on the river with her boat.
screen: `ADRIKA, THE CURSED APSARA.` · `TWINS FOUND IN A FISH.` · `THE KING KEEPS THE BOY.` · `LET HER BE YOUR DAUGHTER.` · then, large: `A KING'S DAUGHTER, A FISHERMAN'S CHILD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, the way a boat settles when the oars rest. Bring to mind the people who raised you, or who stood in for the ones who couldn't: a parent, a grandparent, a foster parent, an aunt, a coach, a neighbor. Let them be as they are, with all their halves. Breathe in, and notice where you came from. Breathe out, and notice the people who took you in along the way. Both are part of the story. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A king's daughter found in a fish, given away as a baby, and raised as the fisherman's own.
Your line: Satyavati. Today, ask someone you know well where they started, and listen to the whole answer. Day seven hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

fork.setup: you're King Uparichara. fishermen bring you twins, a boy and a girl, found inside a fish. what do you do?
options: keep the boy, and give the girl to the fishermen's chief.
fork.reveal: he keeps the boy, who becomes King Matsya, and tells the fisherman: let her be your daughter. she is Satyavati.

original.note: Sanskrit Satyavatī, the name of the girl the fishermen's chief raised: later a queen of the Kurus.

trapdoor: what you thought: Satyavati is a fisherman's daughter.
what it means: she's a king's daughter, born from a fish and raised by a fisherman.
what a scholar hears: the Adi Parva tells her birth from King Uparichara and the apsara Adrika, and her twin becomes King Matsya.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Adivansavatarana Parva (King Uparichara, the hawk, the apsara Adrika as a fish; the birth of Matsya and Satyavati)

notes: All paraphrase. Check in Ganguli's account of Uparichara: the seed caught on a leaf and sent by a hawk to his queen Girika; the second hawk; the fall into the Yamuna; Adrika, an apsara cursed by Brahma to be a fish; the twins found by fishermen; Adrika's release; the king keeping the boy (later King Matsya) and giving the girl to the fishermen's chief.

The king here is named Vasu (Uparichara); he is not one of the eight Vasus of days 704-709. The script calls him 'Vasu, called Uparichara' once and then Uparichara; a Keeper may prefer to use only Uparichara to avoid confusion.
Ganguli says she had the smell of fish from her association with fishermen; the script says only that she carries the smell of fish. The name Matsyagandha is left out.
'Some time later' replaces the text's term for when the fish was caught; no number is given.
Day 717 (already written) picks up with the ferry crossing, Parashara and the boon of fragrance; this day stops before the boat and does not explain the fragrance Shantanu followed on day 710.
howItsDone names gotra recitation in some rites such as weddings; confirm.
Editor (y3 audit): Ganguli has Adrika turned into a fish by a Brahmana's curse, not Brahma's; the teach now says only 'under a curse'. Confirm.

Audit (y3, 707-716): cut the unsourced reading that the poem 'doesn't make her ashamed of either half' (Ganguli notes her fishy smell came from contact with fishermen); replaced with the fact that her birth is told earlier, in the Adivansavatarana Parva's account of the ancestors. Rewrote the garbled close 'tomorrow, before the palace, there's a boat'.
